short: Birth and Death of a Rose
title: Birth and Death of a Rose
tldr: An object is a trajectory through geometry, reflectance and texture. A rose blooming and wilting is one object, and this generates the whole trajectory from 2D priors.

problem.task: Generate temporal object intrinsics — geometry, reflectance and texture evolving over an object's lifespan — from 2D priors alone.

inputs.name: concept
inputs.chars: A natural phenomenon with a life cycle: a blooming rose, a rusting nail.

inputs.name: query
inputs.chars: Any time in the lifespan, any camera, any environment map.

outputs.name: object intrinsics at time t
outputs.chars: Renderable and relightable, not a baked video.

training.supervision: Score distillation from a frozen 2D diffusion model. No 4D ground truth exists for these phenomena.
training.note: Neural Templates for the temporal state are derived automatically from self-supervised image features, which is how consistency across the lifespan is enforced.

method.intuition: Time-varying object identity is a missing axis in 3D asset modeling, and 2D generative priors already contain it if you can hold state consistent while distilling.

experiments.headline: Controllable rendering of a phenomenon from any viewpoint, any lighting and any point in its lifespan.

why: The clean statement of the object-centric premise this list is organised around: objects are defined by how they change.

title: ProcObject-10K: Benchmarking Object-Centric Procedural Understanding in Instructional Videos
tldr: Procedural video benchmarks ask what the person did. This one asks what happened to the object, and models turn out to answer without being able to point at the evidence.

problem.task: Open-ended VideoQA about object preconditions, state evolution, counterfactuals, mistakes and readiness — with temporal grounding of the evidence.

inputs.name: video clip
inputs.chars: 1,799 clips, both egocentric and exocentric, 137 tasks across 9 domains.

inputs.name: question
inputs.chars: One of five reasoning types, all about the object rather than the action.

outputs.name: evidence window
outputs.chars: The interval the answer rests on — scored separately, which is where models fall apart.

training.supervision: Benchmark plus an object-centric SFT baseline with pseudo object-level supervision.
training.note: Fine-tuning transfers to other grounded VideoQA and embodied planning tasks, so the object supervision is not benchmark-specific.

method.intuition: Procedural activity is driven by object state transitions, so a benchmark that never scores object reasoning cannot tell whether a model understands the task or is guessing from language priors.

experiments.headline: A large answering-grounding gap: plausible answers with grounding mIoU below 45%, which exposes reliance on linguistic priors over object dynamics.

why: Turns the object-centric claim into a measurement, and the measurement says current models are not doing it.

title: Particle-Grid Neural Dynamics for Learning Deformable Object Models from RGB-D Videos
tldr: A learned digital twin of rope, cloth and paper bags, fit from sparse RGB-D of a robot poking them, good enough to plan with.

problem.task: Learn action-conditioned dynamics of deformable objects from sparse-view RGB-D, then plan with the learned model.

inputs.name: RGB-D
inputs.chars: Sparse views — 2 to 4 cameras, not a mocap dome.

inputs.name: robot action
inputs.chars: End-effector motion applied to the object.

outputs.name: particle displacement
outputs.chars: Dense per-particle motion; rendered through Gaussian Splatting for visual comparison.

training.supervision: Self-supervised from recorded robot-object interaction videos — no simulator, no material parameters given.
training.note: Category-level generalization to unseen instances comes from the hybrid representation, not from more data.

method.intuition: Particles carry shape and grids carry spatial continuity, so a hybrid keeps both dense prediction and stable learning where a pure particle model would drift.
components: Gaussian Splatting renderer for visual supervision
model-based planning over the learned dynamics

datasets.name: robot interaction recordings: ropes, cloths, stuffed animals, paper bags

experiments.headline: Outperforms both learned and physics-based simulators, most clearly when camera views are limited, and supports goal-conditioned manipulation.

why: Deformables are where explicit physical state stops being optional, and this is the bridge from RGB-D observation to a model you can plan against.

title: Force Prompting: Video Generation Models Can Learn and Generalize Physics-based Control Signals
tldr: Poke a plant or blow wind at a flag by conditioning a video model on a force field. Trained on a handful of Blender scenes, it generalizes to real materials.

inputs.name: image
inputs.chars: A real photo of a scene with something deformable in it.

inputs.name: force prompt
inputs.chars: Either a localized point force at a pixel, or a global wind vector.

outputs.name: video
outputs.chars: The scene responding to that force. No 3D asset or simulator at inference.

training.supervision: Paired force-video data synthesized in Blender over a small set of objects.
training.note: The whole result rests on the gap between that narrow synthetic training set and the diverse real inputs it generalizes to.

method.intuition: A pretrained video model already contains a motion prior for how materials respond. Force conditioning only has to name the input, not teach the physics.

experiments.headline: Generalizes across geometries, settings and materials from limited demonstrations of a few objects.

why: Tests whether a video model has physics or only appearance, by giving it a control signal that only physics can satisfy.

title: PhysX-3D: Physical-Grounded 3D Asset Generation
tldr: Generated 3D assets look right and weigh nothing. This annotates scale, material, affordance, kinematics and function, then generates assets that carry them.

problem.task: Image-to-3D generation that outputs physical properties alongside geometry.

inputs.name: image
inputs.chars: Single view of an object.

outputs.name: 3D asset
outputs.chars: Geometry and texture, quality preserved against a non-physical baseline.

outputs.name: physical properties
outputs.chars: Five dimensions — the ones that decide whether the asset can be simulated or grasped.

training.supervision: PhysXNet, built by a VLM-assisted human-in-the-loop annotation pipeline over existing 3D assets.
training.note: The pipeline is reusable — it turns any raw 3D corpus into a physics-first one.

method.intuition: 3D generation is moving from screens to simulators and robots, and a mesh without mass, material or joints cannot cross that line.

experiments.headline: Plausible physical predictions without degrading native geometry quality.

why: Marks where 3D generation stops being graphics and starts being an input to physical AI.

title: 4D-LRM: Large Space-Time Reconstruction Model From and To Any View at Any Time
tldr: Feed-forward 4D: posed image tokens in, per-pixel 4D Gaussians out, 24 frames reconstructed in under 1.5 seconds instead of a per-scene optimization.

problem.task: Reconstruct a dynamic object from unconstrained views at unconstrained times, and render any new view-time pair.

inputs.name: posed frames
inputs.chars: A few views at a few timestamps; the camera setup need not be fixed.

inputs.name: query
inputs.chars: Any view, any time — including between the observed timestamps.

outputs.name: 4D Gaussians
outputs.chars: Per-pixel primitives, rendered at effectively unbounded frame rate.

training.supervision: Large-scale supervised 4D pretraining on rendered object sequences.
training.note: The claim under test is a scaling claim: does spatiotemporal pretraining generalize the way 3D pretraining did?

method.intuition: Optimization-based 4D is slow and generative 4D is unfaithful. A single feed-forward space-time representation gets both, if it is pretrained at scale.

metrics: PSNR / SSIM / LPIPS on novel view-time
experiments.headline: 24-frame sequences reconstructed in one forward pass in under 1.5 s on a single A100, generalizing to unseen objects and camera setups.

why: Shows the reconstruction side of physical-world modeling following the same scaling recipe as the generative side.

title: 3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering
tldr: Explicit anisotropic Gaussians plus a visibility-aware rasterizer make radiance fields real-time, which is why almost every 4D and digital-twin paper after 2023 is built on them.

problem.task: Novel-view synthesis of a static scene at real-time rates.

inputs.name: camera
inputs.chars: Any pose in the captured volume.

training.supervision: Per-scene optimization against posed photographs, initialized from SfM points.
training.note: Not a learned prior — every scene is fit from scratch, which is exactly what feed-forward successors set out to remove.

method.intuition: Volumetric quality does not require querying an MLP in empty space. Put explicit primitives where the scene actually is and rasterize them.

experiments.headline: State-of-the-art quality with real-time (≥30 fps) 1080p rendering and competitive training time.

why: Background: the representation that made 4D capture of physical scenes cheap enough to be routine.

title: NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis
tldr: A scene is a function from 5D coordinates to density and colour, fit by differentiable volume rendering — the paper that made implicit 3D the default.

problem.task: Novel-view synthesis from a sparse set of posed images.

inputs.name: ray sample
inputs.chars: 5D: position plus viewing direction.

outputs.name: density and radiance
outputs.chars: Composited along rays by classical volume rendering.

training.supervision: Photometric loss against the input images. Camera poses are the only extra input.
training.note: Because volume rendering is differentiable, images alone suffice — no geometry supervision.

method.intuition: Store the scene in the weights of a small continuous function rather than a discrete grid, and the resolution limit goes away.

experiments.headline: Outperformed prior neural rendering on complex geometry and view-dependent appearance.

why: Historical anchor for how the field learned to hold 3D scenes in a differentiable form.

title: HOT3D: Hand and Object Tracking in 3D from Egocentric Multi-View Videos
tldr: 3.7M egocentric frames with mocap-grade 3D poses for hands and 33 objects, from Project Aria glasses and Quest 3.

problem.task: Egocentric 3D hand tracking, model-based 6DoF object pose, and 3D lifting of unknown in-hand objects.

inputs.name: egocentric multi-view
inputs.chars: RGB and monochrome streams from Aria or Quest 3.

inputs.name: gaze + point cloud
inputs.chars: Synchronized; scene point clouds and camera poses provided.

outputs.name: hand pose
outputs.chars: In both UmeTrack and MANO parameterizations.

outputs.name: object pose
outputs.chars: Against scanned meshes with PBR materials.

training.supervision: Ground truth from an optical marker mocap system, so poses are metric rather than estimated.
training.note: 19 subjects, 33 rigid objects, kitchen / office / living-room activities beyond pick-and-place.

method.intuition: Multi-view egocentric capture removes the depth ambiguity that makes single-camera hand-object tracking unreliable, and having both a research prototype and a shipped headset makes the benchmark realistic.

experiments.headline: Multi-view methods significantly outperform their single-view counterparts on all three tasks.

why: The measurement ground truth for hand-object interaction, from the viewpoint the human-embodiment branch actually uses.

title: AffordanceLLM: Grounding Affordance from Vision Language Models
tldr: Affordance grounding generalizes when you stop training a segmentation head from scratch and borrow the world knowledge already inside a VLM.

problem.task: Given an image and an action, segment the region of the object you would touch to do it.

inputs.name: image
inputs.chars: In-the-wild internet photos, including unseen objects.

inputs.name: action
inputs.chars: "cut", "hold", "sit on" — may be unseen at training.

training.supervision: Weakly-supervised affordance annotations from AGD20K, with the VLM backbone frozen or lightly tuned.
training.note: The generalization claim is tested by holding out both objects and actions.

method.intuition: Affordance needs knowledge about function that is not visible in the pixels, and a pretrained VLM already carries it.

experiments.headline: Large gains on the AGD20K hard split and affordance grounding for objects and actions never seen in training.

why: Affordance is the natural join between modeling an object and acting on it, which is why it shows up on both sides of this list.

title: SNOW: Spatio-Temporal Scene Understanding with World Knowledge for Open-World Embodied Reasoning
tldr: VLMs have semantics without geometry and point clouds have geometry without semantics. SNOW fuses them into a queryable 4D scene graph with no training at all.

problem.task: Build a persistent, queryable 4D scene representation that a VLM can reason over.

inputs.name: RGB
inputs.chars: Synchronized with the point cloud.

inputs.name: point cloud
inputs.chars: From the robot's depth sensor.

outputs.name: 4D scene graph
outputs.chars: Object nodes carrying semantic, geometric and temporal attributes, anchored globally by SLAM.

training.note: Every component is an off-the-shelf model. The contribution is the interface between them.

method.intuition: Neither the semantic nor the geometric channel is sufficient alone, and fusing them into a persistent graph is a plumbing problem rather than a learning problem.

experiments.headline: Training-free 4D scene understanding that lets a VLM read spatial structure and temporal dynamics directly off the graph.

why: The symbolic-graph answer to world modeling, sitting opposite the latent and pixel answers on the same axis.

title: MindCube: Spatial Mental Modeling from Limited Views
tldr: Ask a VLM about space it cannot see and it guesses. Make it draw a cognitive map first and then reason on the map, and accuracy jumps 20 points.

problem.task: Answer questions about layout, perspective and what-if motion from a handful of views that do not cover the scene.

inputs.name: views
inputs.chars: 3,268 images; deliberately partial coverage of the space.

inputs.name: question
inputs.chars: 21,154 questions over position, orientation and mental simulation.

outputs.name: cognitive map
outputs.chars: Intermediate — an explicit internal layout the model generates before answering.

training.supervision: Supervised fine-tuning on map-then-reason traces, then reinforcement learning.
training.note: The ablation is the point: unseen intermediate views, language chains and cognitive maps are compared head to head.

method.intuition: Humans reason about unseen space by building an internal model first. Making that step explicit and trainable is what closes the gap.

experiments.headline: Existing VLMs score near random. Map-then-reason lifts 37.8% to 57.8%, and adding RL reaches 61.3%.

why: Locates a specific missing capability — representing space you have not observed — that every embodied system silently assumes.
